Article content Members of the Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) Upper Ottawa Valley Detachment stopped a vehicle travelling 120 km/h in an 80 km/h zone during proactive traffic enforcement on Highway 60 in Killaloe-Hagarty-Richards Township on the evening of July 20. Play Video Article content Police determined the driver was prohibited from operating a motor vehicle and had consumed alcohol. A 38-year-old man from Wilno was charged with operation while prohibited under the Criminal Code, operation while impaired (80 plus), speeding contrary to the Highway Traffic Act, failing to surrender an insurance card and failing to surrender a permit for a motor vehicle. The accused is scheduled to appear in the Ontario Court of Justice in Pembroke on Aug. 18. His driver’s licence was also suspended for 90 days and the vehicle was impounded for 45 days. During the same investigation, police determined a passenger was in breach of court-imposed conditions. A 36-year-old woman from Killaloe was charged with failure to comply with a release order and was held in custody pending a bail hearing. The OPP reminds motorists to obey posted speed limits, never drive while impaired and ensure they are properly licensed and authorized to operate a motor vehicle. Anyone with information regarding impaired driving is asked to contact the OPP at 1-888-310-1122. In an emergency, call 911. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: The NSW ombudsman has raised concerns about the number of prenatal reports about high-risk children that were not referred on due to a lack of resources. Photograph: yang5i/Getty Images/iStockphoto View image in fullscreen The NSW ombudsman has raised concerns about the number of prenatal reports about high-risk children that were not referred on due to a lack of resources. Photograph: yang5i/Getty Images/iStockphoto New South Wales politics More than a third of prenatal reports to NSW protective services not investigated, ombudsman finds Other families have been unlawfully compelled to be case-managed without consent, watchdog finds Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Sarah Collard Indigenous affairs correspondent Tue 1 Sep 2026 20.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 20.36 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google More than a third of all reports raising concerns about the future welfare of unborn children were closed due to a shortage of allocated caseworkers, while families were unlawfully compelled to take part in prenatal case work, the New South Wales ombudsman has found. In its findings after investigating the Department of Communities and Justice’s practice of responding to prenatal reports, which were released on Friday, the watchdog raised concerns about the number of reports about particularly high-risk children that were not referred on to further support services or a dedicated case manager due to a lack of resources. Birth alerts are meant to help children at risk of abuse. They are routinely used against Aboriginal mothers Read more Under the Care Act, people who suspect a child may be at risk of significant harm after their birth can make a prenatal report to the department. “Our investigation found that DCJ closes a significant number of pre-natal reports without allocation and without referrals to support services, because of ‘no capacity to allocate’,” the NSW ombudsman, Paul Miller, wrote in the report. According to the ombudsman’s report, DCJ data showed that out of 5,007 prenatal reports, 37% or 1,844 were closed without being allocated to a caseworker. Almost half of prenatal reports about unborn children screened as being at risk of significant harm (Rosh) were closed for the same reason while 50% were referred for case management by the department. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The investigation also revealed that child protection services wrongly assumed that its legislative powers were the same for both unborn children and children after birth. Any active case management requires the consent and the knowledge of the pregnant woman or the families – something that was not routinely sought, Miller found. “Any engagement by prospective parents with DCJ following a pre-natal report is, if there are no other children in the household, as a legal matter, entirely voluntary ,” the report said. “DCJ has no statutory power to compel parents to engage with it, including to attend interviews, permit home visits, respond to questions, undertake drug testing or accept service referrals.” The report author acknowledged the “unavoidable tension” between making it clear that families should not be coerced into involvement with child protective services and the fact that their “non-engagement” can later be used as a factor against the family if welfare concerns are raised after the child is born. Miller said the legislation does not allow the department to conduct family meetings, home visits or checks for risks of substance abuse without a family’s consent during pregnancy. “The law does not give DCJ the power to undertake any non-consensual casework during pregnancy. The law also does not allow DCJ to pre-emptively make and act on statutory decisions, such as by deciding that a child needs care and protection warranting removal or other statutory intervention, before the child is born.” He stressed that the DCJ cannot lawfully substantiate Rosh before a child is born but that in some cases that was “routine”, as was the use of risk assessment tools which have previously been reviewed over concerns of racial biases . Dr Jacynta Krakouer, a Noongar woman and the Aboriginal strategy and engagement lead at Adelaide University’s Australian Centre for Child Protection, said First Nations children were overrepresented in both the child protection system and prenatal risk alerts. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “In 2023-24, the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare child protection data shows that 648 unborn reports were substantiated in NSW – 42% of these reports were for unborn Aboriginal babies,” Krakouer told Guardian Australia. While she said pregnancy was a unique opportunity to assist and support women and their families, she cautioned against assumptions a baby might already be at risk before they were born. “There is a big difference between identifying concerns during pregnancy and making a formal finding that an unborn baby is already at risk of significant harm. “At this point, parents haven’t even had the opportunity to demonstrate how they will care for that baby. We need to be very careful about predicting that someone will ‘fail’ as a parent before they have even had the opportunity to parent.” She said the structured decision-making tool used to assess Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander families was not “objectively fair or accurate”. “When previous child protection involvement becomes evidence of future risk, decades of greater surveillance of Aboriginal families can feed into decisions about the next generation. That risks creating a cycle where past involvement with child protection becomes a reason for further involvement with child protection.” The ombudsman said the department had made a number of changes during the course of its investigation, including to explicitly state that the purpose of any engagement was to ensure families were better supported to reduce contact with the child protection system, and were fully informed about consent. The DCJ told the ombudsman it was reviewing its prenatal birth alert system with the Aboriginal community-controlled child safety sector. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4gl.text: Image source, Israel Defense Forces Image caption, The Israeli military said it blew up more than a mile of tunnels By Jessica Rawnsley Published 11 September 2026, 12:34 BST Updated 5 minutes ago Israel's military says it has destroyed a large underground complex operated by Hezbollah in southern Lebanon. It said it used more than 1,000 tonnes of explosives to destroy two tunnels spanning more than 2km (1.2 miles) beneath the Ali Taher Ridge. The blast triggered seismic activity equivalent to a magnitude 4.1 earthquake, according to the US Geological Survey. There was no immediate public response from Hezbollah or the Lebanese government. Israeli forces took control of the ridge last week after months of fighting with the Iran-backed group there. The Israeli military occupies a large swathe of southern Lebanon captured after the conflict with Hezbollah resumed in March. Images released by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) showed a fireball lighting up the sky. "The sky lit up and about 15 seconds later we heard the terrifying sound," Ahamed, a resident in Nabatieh, about 6km west of the ridge, told the BBC. "The house shook all together as if it was literally an earthquake." He said people were screaming and children were crying, and that cars filled the roads as people left the area for Beirut. Tremors were even felt in the coastal city of Saida 40km north. The IDF said the underground infrastructure included a command centre used by Hezbollah's Badr unit and contained dozens of rockets, missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles, as well as anti-tank weapons, mines and explosives. "This was strategic infrastructure that was constructed over two decades, funded and planned by the Iranian terror regime," the IDF said in a statement on Telegram. "All of the terrorists who were inside the infrastructure were eliminated or fled." The IDF said the destruction of the complex completed a mission to destroy eight tunnels and establish a "security zone" in the area. The latest action comes amid renewed fighting in southern Lebanon, where Israeli forces have expanded operations against Hezbollah positions and continue to hold what Israel describes as a security zone near the border. Lebanese media reported fresh Israeli strikes elsewhere in the south on Thursday, including Nabatieh al-Fawqa and Mansouri in the Tyre district. The Lebanese army has increased deployments in areas outside Israeli control, including the southern city of Nabatieh, in efforts to strengthen stability and reassure residents, local television station MTV reported. Lebanon was drawn into the war between Israel, the US and Iran on 2 March, when Hezbollah launched rockets into Israel in retaliation for a strike that killed Iran's supreme leader. Israel responded by launching a bombing campaign across Lebanon and invading a significant part of the country's south. Its forces continue to occupy roughly 5% of Lebanese territory. Fighting decreased following a ceasefire deal between Iran and the US in June, alongside a separate agreement between Lebanon and Israel. While hundreds of thousands of people have returned to their homes in Lebanon in the last few months, about 330,000 remain displaced as a result of the conflict, according to the United Nations. Under the Lebanon-Israel framework, Hezbollah is expected to disarm, Israeli forces to withdraw gradually from southern Lebanon and the Lebanese army to deploy across the area. Hezbollah was not directly involved in the agreement and has rejected direct negotiations. Despite a reduction in fighting, Israeli strikes and demolitions in southern Lebanon have continued. At least 4,383 people - including 395 women and 259 children - have been killed in Lebanon by Israeli attacks since 2 March, according to the health ministry, whose figures do not differentiate between combatants and civilians. At least 29 have been killed this week, the ministry says. Israeli authorities say 40 Israeli soldiers and four civilians have been killed in the same period. https://www.politico.eu/article/arrested.text: BERLIN — Former German intelligence chief August Hanning angrily challenged his successor after learning that the agency he once headed, the BND, had passed allegations that he was a Russian spy to investigators. In a three-page letter sent on Aug. 17, less than three months before his arrest this week, Hanning demanded answers to 11 questions from BND President Martin Jäger. In the letter, obtained by WELT — which, like POLITICO, is part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network — Hanning complained that the BND had passed allegations by a former intelligence agent that he was a Russian spy to investigators without consulting him. Advertisement Advertisement Jäger did not respond to the letter at the time, according to Hanning, who spoke to WELT before his arrest. Hanning’s subsequent arrest, including on suspicion of attempted treason, has caused considerable concern abroad. Grzegorz Malecki, the former head of Poland’s foreign intelligence service, told WELT that the case was “extremely concerning” and could deepen allies’ distrust of the BND. He warned this had the potential to undermine intelligence-sharing with Germany. The BND has also raised eyebrows within Germany’s intelligence community over allegations that it allowed Hanning’s former chief of staff, who is also in custody, to work for Hanning outside his official duties. While civil servants are generally permitted to take on outside employment, any approval allowing a member of the BND to work for Hanning would have had to be decided at the senior management level, said Günter Heiss, a former intelligence coordinator under former Chancellor Angela Merkel. “Without knowing the details, I would never have approved anything like this had I been in a position of responsibility at the BND.” Bernd Schmidbauer, a former minister of state and intelligence coordinator under Chancellor Helmut Kohl, told WELT that Hanning had made major contributions to Germany’s national security. The affair was therefore “not only a tragedy for the German intelligence services, but also for the former senior official himself,” Schmidbauer said. Hanning was among Schmidbauer’s closest aides during the 1990s and went on to lead the BND from 1998 to 2005. Dirk Banse is an investigative reporter at WELT. Philipp Fritz is WELT’s Eastern Europe correspondent. Uwe Müller is a freelance reporter based in Berlin. The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network harnesses the resources of the company’s newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces and analysis. It allows journalists — including those from POLITICO, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, Onet, The Telegraph, and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms: online, print, TV and audio. https://praguemonitor.com/pm/business-ec.text: Czechia Business Prague Housing Europe & World Work & Life Briefings Key points Czech companies keep full double-entry accounts under the Accounting Act, while many sole traders may use simpler tax records (daňová evidence). Year-end brings financial statements (balance sheet, profit and loss, notes) whose scope depends on the size category of the business. Accounting records must be kept in Czech, for periods set by law, in a form that supports tax returns and inspections. On this page 8 sections Full accounting or tax records How double entry works Size categories Year-end statements Records, language and retention What your accountant needs from you Software and the accountant Where to check A foreign founder's first meeting with a Czech accountant tends to hold one surprise. The books are kept in Czech, to Czech rules, and your home-country system will not simply be adapted. Accounting here is a legal discipline with its own statute, categories and vocabulary. Knowing the outline beforehand makes the meeting shorter and the invoice smaller. Czech law offers two broad ways of keeping a business's records. Which one you get is partly your choice and partly the law's. Full accounting or tax records? Feature Účetnictví Daňová evidence Law Accounting Act (no. 563/1991 Coll.) Income Tax Act (no. 586/1992 Coll.) Who Companies; some other entities; sole traders in defined cases; others voluntarily Individuals not obliged to keep full accounts Method Double entry Income, expenses, assets and receivables as the tax rules require Output Balance sheet, profit and loss account, notes Enough to calculate the income tax base; no balance sheet The choice is not always free. Confirm with an accountant before the first invoice. Full accounting or tax records Full accounting ( účetnictví ) is governed by the Accounting Act (no. 563/1991 Coll.) and its implementing decrees. It is double-entry bookkeeping: every transaction lands in at least two accounts, assets and liabilities appear on a balance sheet, and income and costs form a profit and loss account. Companies such as the s.r.o. and a.s. must use it, as must some other entities and sole traders in defined circumstances. Others adopt it voluntarily. Tax records ( daňová evidence ) are the simpler option for individuals who are not obliged to keep full accounts. They track income and expenses, plus assets and receivables as the tax rules require, and they are enough to calculate the income tax base. They produce no balance sheet. The Income Tax Act (586/1992 Coll.) says what they must contain. Our guide to becoming an OSVČ shows where this fits. A sole trader using flat-rate expenses may keep an even lighter record of income. The choice is not always free, so confirm which applies to you before the first invoice goes out. How double entry works You do not need to become a bookkeeper to follow the structure. A company works from a chart of accounts, usually built on the standard Czech one, which groups accounts by type: fixed assets, stock, receivables and payables, bank accounts, equity, costs and revenues. Each transaction gets a debit and a credit. The accountant draws up a trial balance and then the statements. Everything rests on source documents. An invoice, a bank statement, a contract, a payroll sheet: each entry needs one, and the Accounting Act lists what a proper accounting document contains. An expense without paper behind it is an expense an inspector can disallow. Size categories The Act sorts businesses into micro, small, medium and large entities using criteria such as total assets, net turnover and average headcount. A business moves into a category by meeting a set number of those criteria over consecutive periods. The category decides how detailed the statements are, whether the notes can be shortened, whether a management report is needed and, through a related rule, whether an audit is required. We cover the last point in audit requirements . The thresholds sit in the Act and have been adjusted in recent years. Use the current figures from the official source (as of 2026; check the official source), not the ones in last year's blog post. The accounting year in outline Keep source documents Invoices, bank statements, contracts and payroll sheets behind every entry. Book regularly Monthly bookkeeping on a chart of accounts, in Czech. Close the period Reconcile, accrue, value assets and write off bad debts. Prepare the statements Balance sheet, profit and loss account and notes, in the format your size category requires. Approve and file Owners approve; companies deposit the statements in the register. Year-end statements The year-end set, the účetní závěrka , normally has three parts: the balance sheet ( rozvaha ), the profit and loss account ( výkaz zisku a ztráty ) and the notes ( příloha ). Micro entities use shorter formats, while larger ones add a cash flow statement and a statement of changes in equity. The statements are prepared under Czech accounting standards or, for certain entities, international ones. Owners or the general meeting approve them, and companies then file them in the commercial register. That step has its own article: annual accounts filing . The accounting period is usually the calendar year. A different 12-month financial year is possible, but it has to be justified and reported to the tax office, and it moves your deadlines, so decide early. The books are yours The business stays responsible even when an outside accountant keeps them. Make sure you can always get them back if the relationship ends. Records, language and retention Records must be kept in Czech, although you can keep supplementary versions in another language alongside. Electronic records are allowed if they stay readable and protected against loss. Retention periods differ by document type: statements and ledgers are kept longer than routine supporting papers, and tax law has its own limitation periods, which can be longer still. Look up the current periods with the Financial Administration or your accountant. What your accountant needs from you Accounting is a collaboration, and the data flows one way. The accountant cannot book what they have not seen, so the quality of the books is the quality of your document habit. The documents are not mysterious: every purchase invoice and receipt, every sales invoice, bank statements, contracts that create obligations, payroll records, and the minutes of significant decisions. If you can say on which day each month they reach the accountant, you have solved most late-filing risk. A tip from the other side of the desk: send documents in the form the accountant prefers, named and dated, with a one-line note on anything unusual. A payment of unclear purpose sitting in a bank statement costs more to explain in March than it does to label in May. Treat the accountant's questions as a mirror of what an inspector would ask. Software and the accountant Most small companies use accounting software with Czech localisation, VAT handling and a connection to the tax portal. If you are a VAT payer, check that it can produce the control statement format described in how to file a VAT return . A good accountant explains choices in plain terms, quotes in writing and tells you what papers they need and when. Ask what the fee covers: monthly bookkeeping, payroll, VAT returns, the annual return, the year-end statements. Late documents from the client are the most common cause of late filings, which is awkward for a profession that gets blamed for them. Before the first bookkeeping month, write a one-page note: which system you use, which software, who keeps the documents, the day each month receipts go to the accountant, and the year-end date. Send it to the accountant and ask for corrections. A clear process saves more than a cheap fee. Where to check The Accounting Act and its implementing decrees are the source for double-entry accounting, the Income Tax Act for tax records, and the Financial Administration explains the filing side. For the size categories and retention periods, use the current text and the accountant's confirmation. Frequently asked questions Must records be in Czech? Yes, though you can keep supplementary versions in another language alongside. Electronic records are allowed if they stay readable and protected against loss. Do small businesses need a balance sheet? Those using full accounting do. Micro entities use shorter formats, and sole traders using tax records produce no balance sheet. Can I choose a different financial year? A different 12-month year is possible, but it has to be justified and reported to the tax office, and it moves your deadlines. Where do the size categories come from? The Accounting Act sorts businesses into micro, small, medium and large using criteria such as total assets, net turnover and average headcount. This is a general explainer, not legal or tax advice. Rules change; check the official source or a licensed adviser. The Eastern Flank Working in Romania New Names on the Cover The Cooking Show Expat in Romania RRI Special The Sounds of Romania Voices from the Archives Our Shows Listeners’ Corner Romanian without Tears Sunday Show In the Spotlight Through the Looking Glass Change Makers Happening in Romania Music Time Artscape Weekend Edition On demand LISTEN HERE Useful information Things to know How to listen Forum QSL QSL-cards Homepage » Actualitate » The Week in Review » 12-17 October, 2026 12-17 October, 2026 A look at the main headline-making events this past week The Week in Review Corina Cristea , 17.10.2026, 14:00 A new government for Romania Romania moved a step closer to a new government on Thursday, when Prime Minister-designate Luca Niculescu submitted his governing programme and proposed cabinet. Niculescu, a diplomat and former journalist, said the line-up was unusual for Romania but reflected the country’s current circumstances: 17 ministers, including a deputy prime minister, with 11 drawn from the Social Democratic Party (PSD) and six independent experts, some in key posts such as finance and foreign affairs. The cabinet is expected to receive the backing of the PSD, the National Liberal Party (PNL), the Democratic Union of Ethnic Hungarians in Romania (UDMR) and MPs representing national minorities. Parliamentary committee hearings for the proposed ministers and a confidence vote at a joint sitting of both houses are scheduled for early next week. “After months of political crisis, we need a government that can take swift decisions and address economic and social problems that can no longer wait,” Niculescu said. The incoming government’s immediate priorities will include revising the budget to prevent disruption to hospital operations, medicine supplies and payments to local authorities and businesses; adopting the 2027 budget before the end of the year; helping vulnerable people meet their bills this winter; reviving the economy and supporting Romanian businesses; and improving revenue collection, the prime minister-designate added. In foreign policy, its objectives include completing Romania’s accession to the OECD and negotiating more effectively to advance the country’s interests. Financial markets reacted positively: Romania’s government borrowing costs fell significantly, the stock market rose by almost 2%, and the national currency strengthened against the euro. President Nicușor Dan in Brussels Attending the European Council meeting in Brussels on Thursday and Friday, President Nicușor Dan called for an “ambitious” EU budget for 2028–2034. According to Romania’s Presidential Administration, Bucharest wants the EU budget to maintain funding levels for cohesion policy and the Common Agricultural Policy. Both are essential to narrowing development gaps between member states, modernising agriculture, developing rural communities and strengthening food security. Romania is also calling for funding to strengthen European defence capabilities, with particular attention to the eastern flank and the strategically important Black Sea region, as well as policies to restore competitiveness and reduce strategic dependencies in energy and advanced technologies. Ahead of the summit, President Dan and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni co-chaired a meeting of the Friends of Cohesion group, which brings together 17 countries opposed to cuts in agricultural and cohesion funding under the next multiannual budget. In Brussels, the Romanian president also met NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte to discuss security in the Black Sea following attacks on merchant vessels in which Russia is suspected of involvement. Following the meeting, also attended by Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev, NATO will convene the North Atlantic Council for consultations on Black Sea security. Sources familiar with the NATO talks say the alliance expects Russia to escalate tensions through various provocations. Rutte said the allies would adapt their deterrence posture in the Black Sea. The i nterim prime minister meets EU ambassadors Romania’s economic situation, energy security and threats in the Black Sea region were on Wednesday’s agenda of talks between the interim Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan and ambassadors from EU member states. “Romania’s EU membership is one of the most important achievements of the past 35 years. Being part of the European family is a major gain for Romania, and I am confident that the country will stay on this course,” Bolojan said. He outlined the measures adopted by the government to balance the budget and address structural weaknesses in the economy, with the aim of strengthening Romania’s economy and boosting business confidence. The interim prime minister stressed the need to continue reforms amid a challenging international environment and highlighted the importance of energy security and keeping prices affordable for households. The discussions also covered security in the Black Sea, hybrid operations and disinformation campaigns. Bolojan thanked the European ambassadors and the European Commission representative for their cooperation and continued support for the Romanian government. He also thanked Romania’s allies for their military presence in the country, stressing its contribution to strengthening NATO’s eastern flank and security in the Black Sea region. Economic forecasts for Romania The IMF has revised downward its forecast for Romania’s economy this year, projecting a contraction of 0.5%, compared with the 0.7% growth it predicted in April, according to its latest World Economic Outlook, published this week. The IMF has also slightly lowered its forecast for Romania’s GDP growth in 2027 to 2.2%. It is also more pessimistic about the country’s progress in narrowing its current account deficit, which it now expects to fall to just 7% of the GDP this year. Meanwhile, Romania’s National Institute of Statistics reported that the trade deficit widened by 1.4% in the first eight months of the year compared with the same period last year.
